subject: Anthropology
title: Excavation Techniques
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Excavation Techniques.

hook.text: Archaeologists don't dig with shovels and luck. They use grids, trowels, and brushes — one centimeter at a time.

buildup.text: Excavation divides a site into a grid. Each square is dug carefully, and every object is recorded in three dimensions.

discovery.text: Soil is sifted through screens to catch tiny finds: beads, seeds, fish bones, and flakes of worked stone.

twist.text: Excavation is destructive. Once a layer is removed, it can never be put back. Every dig is a one-time event.

climax.text: Careful excavation preserves context. Sloppy digging destroys the very information archaeology exists to recover.

punchline.text: You only get one chance to read the ground.

quiz.question: Why is excavation considered destructive?
options: Removing layers destroys the original context permanently

details.summary: Archaeological excavation is a controlled, destructive process — once a site is dug, it cannot be re-excavated. Archaeologists use standardized methods including grid systems, careful layer-by-layer removal, and meticulous recording to preserve maximum information before it is gone forever.
details.whyItMatters: Excavation destroys the very evidence it studies. This makes methodology critical — poor excavation permanently destroys knowledge. The standards archaeologists follow determine what future generations can learn from a site.
takeaways: Excavation is destructive — sites cannot be re-dug once excavated
Grid systems and layer-by-layer removal preserve maximum information
Meticulous recording is essential because the site is destroyed

faq.question: Why do archaeologists leave parts of sites unexcavated?
faq.answer: Since excavation destroys evidence, leaving sections unexcavated preserves them for future researchers with better techniques and questions. Today's best methods will seem crude in fifty years. Preserving portions of sites is responsible stewardship.

faq.question: What tools do modern archaeologists use during excavation?
faq.answer: Tools range from heavy machinery for overburden removal to trowels, brushes, and dental picks for delicate work. Digital tools include GPS mapping, photogrammetry, 3D scanning, and database recording. The appropriate tool depends on what is being excavated.
